title: Automation may interrupt the expected industrial relocation ladder as aging and protectionism intensify
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11468, Can the Flying Geese Fly Again? Automation and the Pattern of Industrialization
geography: China, nine individually reported countries, advanced economies, emerging markets, and World Bank regions in a 16-sector multi-country trade and robotization model

observations.period: Model scenarios calibrated to trade, robot adoption, labor force, and production-network data; China and developing-country comparison

denominator.unit: sectors in the multi-country quantitative model

china_robot_productivity.value: doubling robot productivity raises China's modeled real GDP by 0.77%, compared with 0.23% on average for developing economies

aging_pattern.value: China and Thailand face severe modeled export and GDP declines from aging, while India and the Philippines see significant increases in trade and economic activity

automation_timing.value: earlier robot adoption in China, associated with higher real wages, gives it a stronger modeled response to productivity gains

development_ladder.value: automation can preserve incumbent manufacturing competitiveness rather than allowing production to relocate predictably toward younger or lower-wage economies

observations.method: Multi-country general-equilibrium trade model fitted to global trade, industrial-robot, population, and input-output production-network data.
observations.uncertainty: Results are model scenarios dependent on calibration, functional forms, population projections, trade assumptions, robot productivity, and sector aggregation; they are not observed post-automation outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Manufacturing workers, younger and older labor forces, firms in China and developing economies, exporting sectors, consumers of traded goods, and places competing for industrial relocation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher robot productivity can increase GDP and exports without preserving employment, wages, bargaining power, or broad-based local opportunity; incumbent competitiveness is not equivalent to worker welfare.

denominator.unit: country-group and country comparison results highlighted for trade-cost interactions

china_turkiye.value: doubling robot productivity undoes the modeled negative real-GDP effects of higher trade costs in China and Türkiye

developing_countries.value: a tenfold increase in robot productivity is required in the model to eliminate the harmful real-GDP effects of higher trade costs for all developing countries

advanced_economies.value: advanced economies experience a large modeled decline in exports and GDP in the combined scenario because they are effectively engaging in a trade war

geopolitical_industrialization.value: protectionism and automation do not simply reverse one another; the ability to absorb trade shocks depends on existing robot capability and sector structure

observations.method: Counterfactual combinations of a 10% increase in Northern trade costs and alternative robot-productivity multipliers within the calibrated model.
observations.uncertainty: The tenfold productivity requirement is a model-specific threshold, not a forecast of feasible investment or a universal policy prescription; trade responses may differ with retaliation, subsidies, exchange rates, and firm entry.
observations.subgroup: Export-oriented firms, industrial workers, importing consumers, governments using protection, and developing economies seeking manufacturing-led upgrading.
observations.counterinterpretation: Protection can redirect supply chains even when modeled GDP effects are offset, and robot adoption may deepen concentration if capital, skills, energy, and finance are unevenly available.

observations.period: China labor-force decline and sectoral automatable-task thresholds

denominator.unit: illustrative sectors: vehicles, computer and electronics, and metals

vehicles.value: with about a 10% labor-supply decline, doubling robot productivity can fully offset the loss of comparative advantage in vehicles

electronics.value: maintaining the same outcome in computer and electronics requires about a 220% robot-productivity increase, or more than three-fold productivity

metals.value: when labor-force reduction exceeds 14%, the model cannot identify an equivalent competitiveness-preserving threshold in metals because too few tasks are automatable

worker_conversion.value: the same demographic and technology shock produces different employment and place consequences depending on the task composition of the sector

observations.method: Sector-specific counterfactual analysis varying labor supply, robot productivity, and the estimated share of automatable tasks while holding China's export share constant.
observations.uncertainty: The exercise preserves an export-competitiveness target rather than estimating worker transitions, displacement, wage distribution, or local employment; task shares and productivity thresholds are model inputs.
observations.subgroup: Vehicle, electronics, and metals workers; regions specialized in low-automatable production; firms choosing capital versus labor; and younger economies expecting labor-intensive industrial entry.
observations.counterinterpretation: A sector can preserve export competitiveness while shedding workers or changing job quality; sectors with fewer automatable tasks may retain labor demand but lose competitiveness under demographic pressure.

boundary: This record adds an automation-to-industrial-relocation and sectoral-task-composition mechanism. It is a calibrated multi-country model, not observed causal evidence that automation preserves manufacturing jobs, improves wages, distributes gains, or changes household consumption. The cultural and social consequences remain open: whether the expected development ladder weakens, which places lose industrial entry, and how workers and consumers experience the resulting concentration require country, firm, and worker-level follow-through.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank PDF, document record, document API metadata, reproducibility package, and README were reviewed for the 16-sector model, robot-productivity scenarios, aging and trade-cost interactions, China and developing-country comparisons, and vehicle/electronics/metals task thresholds. The reproducibility package is temporarily embargoed and relies partly on restricted IFR robot data.
